title: Stop an abbreviation's dot from faking a sentence boundary in the citation check
action:
FIX-FIRST. An independent judge returned NEEDS_REVISION on bln-4 with a working counterexample against the citation check — the one check D4 exists for. Close it, red first.

THE DEFECT. `starts_sentence` (blind/mod.rs:685-691) treats ANY '.' followed by whitespace as a sentence boundary, so an abbreviation's dot manufactures a false boundary and a citation can begin just after it, dropping the negation that governs the clause.

The judge's verbatim counterexample, which passes today and must refuse after this cell:
  proposal: "We should not follow lane-b here, i.e. cache the token on the worker side."
  citation: "cache the token on the worker side"
  It resolves, clears both floors (34 chars, 7 words), and inverts the lane's meaning.
The judge confirmed the same hole for `e.g.` and for ASCII `...`, and found one more case that also passes: cross-sentence framing, "Never do the following. Cache the token on the worker side." cited as the second sentence alone. That one lies OUTSIDE the within-sentence contract the plan scoped — decide it explicitly rather than by accident, and say which way you went in the deviations.

WHAT TO DO.
1. Write the failing probes FIRST, one per case: `i.e.`, `e.g.`, ASCII `...`, and the cross-sentence framing case. Run them and see them red before touching the boundary rule. A probe that is green before your fix is not a probe for this defect.
2. Then harden the boundary rule. A dot is a sentence boundary only when the token ending at it is not an abbreviation. Carry a small CLOSED, commented abbreviation set (at least i.e., e.g., etc., cf., vs., no., fig., approx.) and treat a run of two or more dots as never a boundary. If you also require the character after the boundary whitespace to be uppercase in the ORIGINAL proposal text, say so and prove it does not break the existing green whitespace/case-fold probe — `normalize` case-folds, so the boundary test may need the un-normalized text.
3. Keep all 42 existing `verbs::blind` tests green. If any goes red, that is information about your fix, not permission to edit the test.

HONESTY REQUIREMENT — this is a must_have, not a nicety. A mechanical string check CANNOT catch every semantic inversion; the judge broke the first attempt in one pass, and a closed abbreviation set is still a heuristic. Write one comment block above the boundary rule naming exactly what class this check catches and what it cannot, and do NOT let any refusal text or doc line claim the citation check proves a citation is faithful. It proves the quoted span is a whole sentence of the named lane's own bytes. That is the true claim; make the code say only that.

Do NOT weaken the floors, the per-lane scoping, or any other check to make a probe pass.

Two inputs still strip a negation living in the SAME sentence. (1) A LISTED ABBREVIATION WITH ONE ADJACENT CHARACTER: the set lookup at mod.rs:723-724 is byte equality on the space-delimited token, so any leading punctuation defeats it. 'We should not follow lane-b (i.e. cache the token on the worker side.' cited as 'cache the token on the worker side' PASSES; all 28 combinations of leading ( " ' [ - * em-dash : with i.e./e.g./etc./cf. passed. '(i.e. ...)' is the most common written form of the very abbreviation the cell mandated. (2) A NUMERIC OR ALPHA ENUMERATOR: '1.' is not in the set, so 'We must not do any of the following:

1. Cache the token on the worker side.
2. Skip the lease check.' cited as 'cache the token on the worker side' PASSES; same for 'a.' and 'ii.'. Markdown numbered lists under a negated stem are ordinary design prose. The end side mirrors it
